content: Access to healthcare services plays a critical role in determining the health outcomes of populations. Mobile clinics are designed to deliver a variety of healthcare services, with a primary focus in many countries on addressing the health needs of women and children. It is hypothesized that improving access to healthcare through mobile clinics can lead to better health outcomes for these populations. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of mobile clinic services on the health of women and children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases for systematic reviews and primary studies. These included the Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effectiveness (DARE), Health Technology Assessment Database (HTA), NHS Economic Evaluation Database (NHS EED), Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Global Health, POPLINE, and others. The search spanned from February 2014 to May 2016, depending on the database. The review included individual and cluster-randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled trials (non-RCTs), controlled before-and-after (CBA) studies with at least two intervention and two control sites, and interrupted time series (ITS) studies with clearly defined intervention points and sufficient data points before and after the intervention. Mobile clinics were defined as vehicles staffed by healthcare providers (with or without nurses) and drivers, which regularly visited specific areas. The participants included women aged 18 years or older and children under 18 years of age from low-, middle-, and high-income countries. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, extracted data using a standardized form, and assessed the quality of evidence using the GRADE approach. Two cluster-RCTs met the inclusion criteria, both conducted in the United States. The first study evaluated whether offering onsite mobile mammography combined with health education was more effective in increasing breast cancer screening rates compared to providing health education alone, which included reminders to attend a static clinic for mammography. Women who were offered mobile mammography and health education were more likely to undergo mammography within three months of the intervention compared to those in the control group (55% versus 40%; odds ratio 1.83, 95% confidence interval 1.22 to 2.74). However, the certainty of this evidence was low. A cost-effectiveness analysis revealed that the cost per patient screened was higher for mobile units compared to static units. The incremental costs per patient screened were USD 61 for a mobile full digital unit and USD 45 for a mobile film unit. The second study compared asthma outcomes in children aged two to six years who received care from a mobile asthma clinic versus those who received standard care from their usual primary care provider. The findings suggested that children receiving care from the mobile asthma clinic experienced little to no difference in symptom-free days, urgent care visits, and caregiver-reported medication use compared to those receiving standard care. The certainty of this evidence was also low. The authors concluded that the limited evidence and the narrow range of contexts in which studies have been conducted make it challenging to draw definitive conclusions about the impact of mobile clinics on the health of women and children compared to static clinics. Further high-quality research is needed across low-, middle-, and high-income countries to better understand the effects of mobile clinics on these populations.
